title: David Grusch Makes New Claims About Missing Gen. McCasland
excerpt: UAP whistleblower David Grusch makes cryptic new claims about missing Air Force Gen. Neil McCasland during an interview with Joe Rogan.
content:
The UAP whistleblower told Joe Rogan he now understands what McCasland was allegedly “hinting” at years ago, before adding: “I know a lot about General McCasland”

The mysterious disappearance of retired Air Force Maj. Gen. William “Neil” McCasland is back in the spotlight after UAP whistleblower David Grusch made some striking new claims about the missing general during an interview with Joe Rogan.

Appearing on The Joe Rogan Experience on Sept. 30, Grusch was discussing what he claims was a government video showing deceased, human-looking beings recovered from an unidentified craft when he suddenly invoked McCasland. Grusch described the beings as unusually beautiful, with pale or bluish-white skin, before recalling something McCasland allegedly told blink-182 frontman and longtime UFO researcher Tom DeLonge: “Think of the Greek Gods.”

“And now I kind of understand what he meant,” Grusch told Rogan.

The connection became even more explicit later in the interview. When Rogan again referenced the alleged beings as looking like “Greek gods,” Grusch responded, “That’s how I described it,” before adding that it was “clearly” what McCasland had been hinting at to DeLonge.

Grusch then turned directly to McCasland’s still-unsolved disappearance, calling the circumstances concerning, and reminding viewers that the retired general vanished from his Albuquerque-area home in February 2026. McCasland left behind his cellphone and other electronic devices, while his wallet, hiking boots and .38-caliber revolver were missing.

“There’s a lot of reasons why McCasland’s disappearance was very concerning,” Grusch said. “He walked out of his residence in Albuquerque and vanished. Nobody knows what f*cking happened to the guy.”

Grusch specifically pointed to circumstances that have previously been reported by Los Angeles, including McCasland apparently leaving his cellphone behind while one of his firearms was missing.

“It’s, like, very weird,” Grusch said.

He also brought up McCasland’s preparations for a planned trip, saying the retired general was supposed to travel with a group of friends and had gone to REI the day before he disappeared to purchase supplies, including a medical kit. These details track with records previously obtained by Los Angeles from the Bernalillo County Sheriff’s Office. The records included what may be the last confirmed image of McCasland before he vanished: surveillance footage from an REI on Feb. 26 showing the retired general carrying a large white item, a boxed item and what appeared to be a first-aid kit.

Grusch also acknowledged information contained in publicly released police body-camera footage concerning McCasland’s condition before his disappearance. He referenced what McCasland’s wife told investigators and acknowledged that McCasland had experienced some mental-health and age-related issues, though Grusch characterized them as “nothing major.”

Grusch was also careful not to rule out suicide, noting that he had lost friends to suicide during his military career.

“So, I mean, you never know,” he said.

But he repeatedly returned to the timing of the disappearance, noting that it occurred shortly after President Donald Trump issued a directive concerning the declassification of UAP information.

“It’s very bizarre,” Grusch said.

Then he made another cryptic statement: “Just saying, I know a lot about General McCasland.”

Grusch did not elaborate on exactly what he meant by that statement, or provide any evidence connecting McCasland’s disappearance to UAP disclosure, classified programs or the general’s previous work.

In fact, when Rogan raised reports of other scientists with alleged connections to UAP or reverse-engineering programs who had died or disappeared, Grusch pumped the brakes.

“To be fair, it was a little overblown,” Grusch said, adding that he did not believe there was “a ton of correlation.” Interestingly, Grusch is clearly baffled by the McCasland disappearance, but even he stopped short of endorsing the larger theory that the “missing scientists” were all connected.

There remains no publicly confirmed evidence that McCasland’s disappearance was connected to UAPs, classified programs or his former military work. Bernalillo County investigators have previously pushed back on some of the more sensational theories surrounding the case, telling Los Angeles that certain claims circulating publicly were not supported by their investigation.

The FBI’s involvement has added another layer of unanswered questions. Federal agents joined the search for McCasland in early March. But when Los Angeles later sought FBI records concerning the investigation through the Freedom of Information Act, the Bureau declined to provide them.

“We regret that we cannot provide you records regarding a missing person,” the FBI told Los Angeles, administratively closing the request. Los Angeles challenged that decision, but the Bureau upheld its handling of the request following an additional review.

More than seven months after McCasland walked out of his home, his disappearance remains unresolved.
